The Ferreira Street office closed at four, but Dora stayed on to finish the Tunnel Yield tables, because the ministry wanted them by morning and nobody else on the floor could read the old condensation gauges.

There were forty gauges. Each sat in a seam of the abandoned tram tunnels under the plateau, where the walls sweated a little in the cold hours and the sweat ran into a trough and then into a cistern. Dora's job was to convert each gauge's tick count into litres and then into the household allocation for the eleven districts above. The arithmetic was simple. The figures were not.

Gauge nineteen had been reading the same number for six weeks. Not close to the same number. Exactly the same, to the last tick, every morning at six.

She pulled the raw log. Then the maintenance sheet, which said the sensor had been replaced in March. Then the replacement's serial, which matched nothing in the stores register.

At ten past six the next morning the number changed. It went up by four hundred and twelve litres, which was almost exactly what the district had been short, and then the cistern totals for the whole network went down by the same amount, and the billing system, which Dora had never been allowed to touch directly, sent her a line of text: ALLOCATION ADJUSTED. NO ACTION REQUIRED.

She sat for a while with the cursor blinking. Outside, the first trams of the day were grinding along the street above the tunnels, and somewhere beneath them forty small seams were quietly collecting what the walls gave back.

She opened the form for an anomaly report. Field one: gauge. Field two: date. Field three, labelled REMARKS, had a character limit of two hundred.

She wrote: Reading not consistent with sensor output. Source of adjustment unknown. Request review.

She read it over, saved it, and sent it to the queue, where it would sit with nine thousand other reports until someone with a higher clearance opened it, probably never.

Then she went to get her coat, and on the way out she checked the meter by the door, the one that counted how many people came through the office, because it was a habit, and it said what it always said.

The knot came undone twice before Ilse got it right.

"Again," said Opa, without looking up from the eye he was working into the end of the old mooring line. His left hand was wrapped in tape at two fingers. He did most of the work with the right.

She pulled the strands apart and started over. Three strands, each tucked under one and over the next, the way he had shown her, except she kept losing track of which one was on top.

"Count the tucks out loud," he said.

"One, two, three."

"Quieter. The boat behind you can hear."

There was no boat behind her. The lock was empty and the water sat flat and brown between the gates. Across the basin a man in a orange vest was hosing down the winch housing. Opa liked to say that the lock-keeper's real work was waiting, and that rope was what you did while you waited.

She tucked the last strand and pulled. It held, lumpy and wrong, but it held.

"Good," he said. "Now do it so it looks like nothing."

"That's the whole point?"

"That's the point of a good splice. You can't see where the rope stops being two pieces." He took it from her and turned it over in the light. The lump was there, plain as a scar. He ran his thumb along it and frowned, and then he did something she didn't expect. He cut the splice open with his knife and pulled it back apart.

"Hey."

"Do it again. Slower. And this time don't pull until the tucks are all in."

She did it again. And again. The rope got soft at the ends from being handled, and her fingers went raw, and by the fourth try she could feel the strands want to lie down the right way before she forced them.

Opa tapped the ash off his cigarette on the rail. He did not say she was getting it. He just held out his good hand for the line.

She gave it to him. He ran it through his palm once, twice, and then let it drop onto the concrete between them.

It lay flat. You couldn't find the join.

"There," he said, and went back to his coffee, and she stayed where she was with the coiled rope at her feet, pulling each strand gently to see which one would move.

The piano was older than the building's owner and flat by a quarter tone in the middle octave, which Sung-ho could hear but could not yet name.

"Don't touch the pins yet," said his grandfather, Halmoni's husband, who had no name for himself in this flat except Ahjussi and who hummed through his nose when he was thinking. "First listen to the fork."

The tuning fork was steel and older than the piano. Grandfather struck it on his knee, which was the wrong place, Sung-ho thought, and then put the stem on the lid. A pure A came up through the wood into his cheekbones.

"Now the A above middle C," Grandfather said. "Play it. Tell me if the two agree."

They did not agree. Sung-ho said so, and Grandfather said, "Good. Now you know what wrong sounds like. Most people never learn that before they start fixing things."

They worked for two hours. The wrench was called a lever, the felt was called a mute, and the pins were the part that mattered. Each pin had to be turned a hair at a time, and each hair changed the sound only a little, so you had to keep listening after every turn, even after you thought you had it.

At one point Sung-ho's hands ached and he wanted to say it was good enough. Grandfather did not look up. He just tapped the same key again, a little louder, and waited.

By the end, the middle A and the A above it rang with the same hum, the faint shiver of two strings in step. Sung-ho played a fifth and then a third, and the chord sat still in the room like something that had been moved onto a shelf and left there.

"Tomorrow the tenor section," Grandfather said, and put the fork back in its velvet.

Downstairs, the dry-cleaner's shutter was down. Someone had written a phone number on it in marker, and the number had been wiped out and written again.

The piano was older than both of them and had a dead key in the middle, a G that rang like a spoon on a glass. Ada had her grandson sit on the bench and press it while she held the tuning fork against the lid.

"Hit it, then listen to the beat," she said.

Tomas hit it. The fork and the key made a wobble, wah, wah, wah, slow as a clock.

"That's two strings that don't agree. One of them has to move."

"Which one?"

"Whichever you can hear is wrong. Not the one you like less."

He tried the pin with the small wrench. The wobble got faster. He turned it back. Slower again. Ada didn't take the wrench from him. She sat on the arm of the sofa with her cup of tea going cold and counted under her breath.

"Faster means you're getting close. When it stops, you're there."

It took him forty minutes. His thumb went red on the wrench. At one point he said the piano was broken and she said pianos don't break, they drift, and drift is just a message from the room.

When the wobble finally went out of the G and the fork and the key sat together like two people who had stopped arguing, he didn't say anything. He pressed the key again, and then again, to check it wasn't a fluke.

"Now the next one," Ada said, and held out the fork.

The first thing she learned was that the ditch smelled like diesel and warm tar, and that the tar stayed warm long after the sun went down. She had followed a smell that turned out to be nothing, and by the time she turned around the yard was gone and there was only the sound of trucks coming down off the highway like weather.

For four days she ate what the shoulder gave her, which was not much: a hot dog bun, half a chicken sandwich with the pickles still on it, water in the low spot under the guardrail that tasted like the road. A man in a red cap threw a piece of jerky at her and laughed when she flinched. She flinched anyway, then ate it after he drove off.

There was a woman who worked the register at the truck stop, nights, and she started leaving a bowl by the back door. She never called the dog anything. She just set the bowl down and went back inside, and the dog learned to wait until the door clicked before she came out of the weeds. It went on like that for a while.

The woman had a name tag that said Delia and a bad knee she favored on the left, and one night in November she left the back door propped with a paint can. The dog stood in the doorway a long time. Inside smelled like coffee and bleach and something frying, and it was warm, and she could hear the fryer ticking as it cooled.

She did not go in. She took the bowl off the step and carried it back into the weeds with her, and lay down where she could still see the light under the door, and ate, and watched it until Delia turned the sign around and drove off, and then the lot was dark and she was still there.

The gate didn't latch, and that was the whole of it. She was out on the road with her nose down before anyone in the house noticed the latch, and by the time the car started up the hill she was already past the mailbox and gone around the bend where the road drops toward the creek.

She knew the way back the first night. The problem was the rain, which came in hard around ten and washed the ditch and the shoulder and every mark she'd laid down going out. By morning the world smelled like clean water and nothing of her.

There was a man at the end of the second day who put out a bowl of something warm. She ate it and let him touch her ribs, and when he went inside for more she walked off, because the door he left open led to a room that smelled of a dog that had died in it years ago.

She learned the creek, then the field above it, then the road that ran between them. She learned which porch had a cat that would scream and which one left scraps under a loose board. She got thinner and faster and slept with her back against things.

Nobody came with a flashlight calling a name she'd have answered to. That's what the people in the house never understood: she was never lost, only away, and the difference is that lost is something you feel, and away is just where you are until the smell of the road changes under you and you turn.

The dog left the gate open on a Tuesday, or the boy did, depending on who you asked. Nobody in the Pelletier house could say for sure, and that was the first problem with finding him.

By Thursday the flyers had been stapled to every pole between the laundromat and the rail bridge. The photo showed a brown mongrel with one ear folded like a dog-eared page, sitting in a wheelbarrow he had no business sitting in. Mrs. Okafor from number nine said she'd seen something that looked like him near the fish counter at the market, but she also said she'd seen a fox that looked like a cat, so people nodded and kept walking.

On Saturday the boy took his bicycle and rode the long way round the reservoir, past the half-built marina where the cranes never moved, and into the orchard where the rail dogs were supposed to live. He found a dropped sock, a bottle of cough syrup, and a feeding bowl with a name scratched into it that was not Biscuit. He sat on the wall and ate a plum that was mostly wasp.

On Sunday morning a bread van found the dog asleep under the bakery's back shutter, nose tucked into the warm air from the vent, one folded ear inside out. The baker, who did not read flyers, only noticed the dog was thin and gave him the heel of a loaf. Then he noticed the collar, and then the tag, and then he phoned the number before the dog could decide whether to run.

The boy got there on his bicycle in nine minutes and did not say anything, which surprised everyone including him. He just knelt on the wet pavement and let the dog put his whole weight into his chest, bread crumbs and all, and the baker went back inside to the ovens without being asked to.

The dog's name was Pilot, though nobody called him that except the vet, who had written it on the chart in pencil. Pilot had gone out through the gap in the hedge on Tuesday, when the bread van was idling at the bottom of Mill Lane and the driver was whistling the same two notes over and over. By Wednesday night Dana had walked the length of the allotments twice and left a tin of sardines open by the rail gate.

On Thursday the bakery girl said she had seen a dog that looked like him sitting outside the chip shop on Carver Road, waiting for someone who never came out. Dana drove there with the back seat down and a jumper that smelled of her, but the bench was empty, and the man who ran the shop said the dog had got up at four and gone toward the canal, moving the way dogs do when they have decided on something. There was a bin lid on the pavement that had been knocked over, and the bin lid was the only evidence anyone could agree on.

Dana walked the towpath until the light went orange and then grey. She passed two cyclists, a man fishing with a flask, and a boy throwing a ball against the lock gates, and asked each of them the same question. The boy said he thought he had seen a dog swimming, but he also said he was eleven and had been swimming himself that afternoon, so nobody took him seriously. She wrote Pilot's number on the back of a receipt and taped it to the lock gate anyway.

On Friday morning there was a message from a number she did not know: a photo of a brown-and-white dog asleep in a hay barn, with a sentence underneath that said only "is this him? he won't let me close the door." It was not him. It was a spaniel with a torn ear. But Dana saved the photo, and the next time her phone buzzed she was already reaching for her boots, because a stranger had at least taken the trouble to look.

Pilot came home on Saturday, muddy to the elbows, with a length of blue rope knotted around his neck and his tail going like a windscreen wiper. Nobody ever found out who had tied the rope, and Dana stopped asking after the first week. She put the sardine tin away on the top shelf, where it would be safe from anything with a nose.

Nobody saw the gate at the bottom of the Feeney lot swing open. Mrs. Okafor found it that morning when the milk truck was already backing in, and she still had her coat half on. The dog, a brindle mutt named Tuesday because she had come to the shelter on one, was not in the yard.

The first sighting came from Dale at the scrap yard on Route 9. He said a dog had been sitting by the crusher for an hour, eating nothing, looking at the gate like it owed her money. He threw her half a sandwich. She took it, then walked off toward the rail cut, which nobody in town walks toward unless they have a reason.

By the second afternoon the posters had gone up on every pole between the laundromat and the feed store, and each one had a different phone number written in a different hand. Someone added a note that Tuesday likes chicken but will not come if you call her, which was true, and someone else wrote underneath that she also hates being picked up, which was also true, so the pole now said both.

On the third morning a boy named Marcus Hale found her under the loading dock of the grain elevator, curled against a pallet of seed sacks, with a bent tag still on her collar that read TUESDAY and, on the back in faded marker, a phone number that belonged to a man who had moved to Ohio two years earlier. Marcus sat down on the concrete and waited. She watched him for a long time before she came out.

Mrs. Okafor left the gate shut after that, and every evening she set a bowl of chicken on the back step, just in case.

My wife goes up the ladder with a trowel,
dumps a bucket's worth behind the shed
where nothing useful grows. The furnace man

off the grate. I find the winter coats,
shake one out, and a moth drifts to the floor —
dry, weightless, already what it will be.

past the porch light anymore. By eight
the house is dark except the kitchen,
where she's writing next month's numbers down
in the same pen, the same column, the same hand
that paid for all of this.

You fall asleep before I do.
I lie in the dark and take inventory
of the small machines we keep:
the kettle that clicks, the door that sticks in June,
your glasses folded on the shelf you can't reach.

In the morning I will find the milk
set out, no note, the right amount.
This is the whole of it, I think —
not the vows but the maintenance,
the tightening of things that loosen with weather.

I would let the whole house come apart
and rebuild it with my hands each week
if that is what a life with you costs.
I would know your footsteps anywhere,
the particular drag of your left foot when you're tired.

You are already asleep.
The lamp is on. I am not going to turn it off.

The half-moon of your teeth in toast,
your hair gone gray in the drain,
the dent your body holds in the couch
that stays warm an hour after you leave.

because I never learned,
the cough you do twice at the stairs
so I know the light's still off up there.

who last replaced the bulb,
whose turn to hold the trash,
the two of us agreeing without a word
on which side of the bed faces the door.

I have your sweater on the hook,
and the specific weight of your sleeping arm,
and every morning the same tired fact —
that I would do the dishes again.

The city turns over like a sleeper who's finally warm.
The tourists are folded away in the pension towels.
The fado houses are dark, which is a joke on the fado houses,
everyone honest in there at last by going to sleep.

I take the last tram down to the graveyard at Santo Amaro.
This is what we call it. It is only the tram depot
but the trams are lined up in the shed with their lights on,
and the boards turn slow, the same names all night
through the small hours, over and over,
because the power keeps them.
The trams sleep with their eyes open,
which is what you have to do to run a tram.

I see the river, the other thing that works at night.
There is no one in the first car.
I do not mind. The first car is empty, the whole tram is empty,
the river goes past, and I would not trade the running for anything,
the last man on the last car, in the graveyard, waiting for the shed.

The city is not sleeping. The city is counting.

Water climbing a riser to the ninth floor,
a compressor shuddering, catching, running,
the far-off pulsing of a transformer
holding its breath so the lamps can.

Someone opens a tap in a building I will never enter
and I feel it move through the ground like a vein.

The subway steams under the tar
with the hum of something that never once turned off.
The traffic light changes to no one.
It changes back.

A gantry of scaffolds keeps the wind off a face on a wall.
A truck idles at a loading dock, the driver asleep,
hydraulics ticking as they cool.
The bread is already proofing. The ice is already made.

By four the pipes are the loudest thing alive.
Then the water heaters begin, one at a time,
a whole neighborhood of them
waking up under the plaster.

I don't have a voice. I have a pressure.
I have a grid and a hand on the switch.
What I do at night is invisible
and if I stop for an hour
you'll know my name.

slow as a sleeper.

behind a laundromat window, unguarded.

everything I used to know about heat.

with the good chairs and the good quiet

though I am the one who cooked it,
though I am the one who calls.

The unclaimed shelf at the lost property office in Terminal C runs the length of two radiators and holds, right now, a child's crutch, a wedding album in a supermarket bag, a single ice skate, and the Kindle I am trying not to look at.

The office smells like other people's suitcases. Teri runs it with a mug that says NOT A GUEST and a stapler she won't explain. She says the crutch went home last Tuesday. A boy on crutches ran the whole concourse to make his flight, and left the crutch on the seat, and came back two weeks later with his mother to get it, and cried, which she says happens more than you'd think.

I ask her what the record is. Longest anything has sat here. She doesn't look up from the log.

The album, she says. Four years in March.

It's got eight people in it. Somebody's whole family at a beach. A man in a wheelchair at the front, my age, maybe older. Everyone's wearing the same color, that hard yellow, and the light is so bright on them the color has gone flat and white in the middle. Nobody's called about it. She says when something hits four years, it goes in the bin, and the album hits four in March, and she has already decided she's taking it home instead and not telling anyone, not even the man from procurement, who does not, she says, need an opinion about a family.

The Kindle was left in seat 14A on a flight that came in at 11:44 and turned around for Tulsa at 12:30. Whoever had it was reading a book about a lighthouse. Page two hundred and something. They were almost finished. I keep thinking about what it would cost to just get to the end of your book, and how the person looked at the seat and decided, no, it's fine, and walked the jet bridge with the other people, toward whatever was waiting.

The crutch is gone, so the shelf isn't all sadness. That's what Teri would tell you if you asked. The kid came back for it. You just don't hear about the Tuesdays.

Subject: we'll bring it over today

The bookstore has a delivery radius now, and I think it's about four miles. We haven't measured it exactly, we've just been drawing it on a map in the back and it comes out about that far.

Same-day delivery, within the city, on books we have on the shelf. Order before 2pm and it's a person on a bike or in a car with a bag of books, coming to your door, usually within a few hours. It's a flat fee, five dollars, and free if you're buying more than forty dollars' worth.

What this is really for: you're forty pages from the end of something and you already know you can't start the next one tomorrow. Or the book you need is the one your book club picked and the meeting is tonight. Or you're buying a present and you've left it late, which is the traditional way. Those are the ones worth the five dollars.

What it isn't for: if you're not sure you want it, order it from us anyway and we'll get it to you in a couple of days, or don't, and come in and flip through it. We're not trying to rush anybody.

The shelf is the real limit. We have a small store, and if the book isn't here, same-day doesn't help. There's a search on the site that shows you what's actually in the shop, and if it says it's here, it's here, on a shelf, not in a warehouse.

The radius is the whole city, doesn't reach the towns outside it. If you're not sure you're in it, put your address in at checkout and it'll tell you before you pay.

Two people are doing the deliveries. On a good day you'll get your book before we finish counting the drawer.

— Marguerite
Bookends, on the corner past the laundromat

It works because libraries are the last free place where you can be bad at something in public without buying anything.

3. **Seat Squatting.** No event, no program: a card table of free snacks near the entrance, and every chair on the second floor is fair game to claim and defend for the whole afternoon. Word of a place you can sit for four hours without being asked to move travels faster than any poster.

4. **The Unwanted Shelf.** Books nobody has borrowed in three years, VHS tapes, old yearbooks, donated CDs, laid out with no explanation and no checkout limit for the first hour. The appeal isn't the stuff, it's that the library is admitting it doesn't know what's good either.

5. **Bring Your Adult.** Teens drag a parent, coach, older sibling or grandparent in and make them do one thing the teen is already good at — a game, a repair, a résumé. The teen runs the room; the adult gets a visitor sticker and no vote.

The dog had been gone eleven days when Marisol stopped putting the food bowl out. She had kept it filled at first, then half, then just a spoon to keep the smell, watching the door the way you watch a phone that doesn't ring. On the twelfth night she washed the bowl and put it back in the cupboard, above the one she never used.

The lots behind the auto-parts row were the kind of place a dog could move through without being seen. Chain-link, then a ditch of dry needles, then a fence with one panel bent low where somebody's kid had been climbing it for years. Marisol walked it after her shift, four a.m., the sodium lights going orange at the edges. She was the only one out. She carried a flashlight she didn't turn on.

A man who fixed riding mowers on the corner told her he'd seen a shepherd mix moving the trash cans near the bus shelter. He couldn't say which shelter. He'd been busy. She thanked him and walked to the one on Delgado anyway, then the one by the school, and found nothing but a flattened Coke cup and the smell of wet cardboard.

You stop calling its name out loud after a while. You do it in your head, in the rhythm of the steps: Lolo, Lolo, Lolo, all the way home, all the way back. The name gets thin. It sounds less like a dog and more like a word you've said too many times.

On the eighteenth day a woman from two blocks over left a note on Marisol's screen door: a brown dog had been sleeping under her porch since the cold snap, wouldn't come out. Marisol knelt in the wet gravel and didn't reach in. She just talked, low, about nothing, about the weather. Something in there shifted. She stayed until the porch light came on above her and the woman asked if she wanted coffee. Marisol said yes. It wasn't her dog. She drank the coffee anyway.

1. **The hallway swap.** For one day, everyone works from a chair that isn't theirs — a backend engineer in the support queue, a designer in the billing inbox. The point isn't empathy theater; it's that the offsite produces a written list of the three handoffs that keep breaking, with names attached.

2. **Ship something broken by Friday.** Two teams get 26 hours and one deliberately half-built product — a login page with no password reset, a checkout with no refund path — plus the real bug reports from last quarter. They fix what they can and present the parts they couldn't fix, which is the actual skill most teams never practice out loud.

3. **The bad-decision audit.** Each team brings three past decisions that aged badly, and the room reconstructs what people believed at the time. It works because nobody presents a success story, so the second day's planning starts from what the team gets wrong, not what it wants to be true.

4. **One-ticket day.** Everyone spends half of day one doing a single real support ticket end to end, from the customer's first message to the close-out. Day two is a rewrite of the onboarding doc using only what that ticket taught them, which usually means cutting half of it.

5. **The room that isn't the venue.** The offsite happens in the office, but the team eats lunch somewhere within walking distance they've never been, and each pair comes back with one thing about the neighborhood the company could use — a cheaper supplier, a candidate, a place to hold interviews. Cheapest option here, and the only one that leaves a trace after Friday.

What's the one thing that actually went wrong on the team this year — a missed deadline, a bad hire, a feature nobody used? Each of these themes fixes a different one.

1. Fix the Thing Everyone Works Around
Pick the three recurring annoyances people mention in one-to-ones, such as a broken handoff or a meeting nobody needs, and spend the day making a concrete change to each. It works because teams stop talking about problems when they can see someone acting on them.

2. The Week You Had to Do Each Other's Job
Each person spends an hour shadowing a colleague whose work they know least, then reports back on one thing they did not expect. It works because the fastest way to see why a handoff fails is to sit in the other chair for an hour.

3. Decide Less, Argue Better
Give the group three real open decisions from the past quarter and make them argue for the option they would not have picked. It works because people who have been forced to defend the other side tend to make later calls faster and with less grudge.

Ask each team to list what it produces that a customer would miss, and what it produces that only the company would miss. It works because it gives people a plain, shared sense of what their work is actually for.

Put the group on one physical task with a clear end state, like assembling a bench for the office or running a shared lunch from a single kitchen. It works because a task with a visible result gives people something to talk about beyond their roles, and the result stays in the office afterward.

final:
The tide in Marrow Bay does not go out. It stays where it stopped, at the height of a bad afternoon, and the people built around that: stilt streets, rope ferries between roofs, a whole trade in salvaged ground-floor furniture. Nobody remembers the day it stopped, only that their grandparents had gardens.

The playable part is the debt. Every household owes hours to the Pump Houses, the crews that keep the water from creeping higher by hauling silt out of the old river mouth. final: Mo is the cat who keeps the log at Gull Point lighthouse, a tally in pencil of every boat that passes the rock, written in the margin beside the keeper's entries. One foggy night a foreign freighter sounds its horn twice, then goes quiet, and Mo finds, pinned to the lamp room door, a ship's list of crew with one name crossed out and "cat, unrecorded" written underneath. Believing the list is a mistake, Mo spends the next week trying to get the harbour office to correct it, climbing the stairs of the mail boat, sitting on the wrong desks, and bringing back a reply in each case that someone else has just added one more to the list. By the end, the book's question is simply who gets counted and who counts them, and the answer Mo writes in her own log is a single line with her paw print under it.

A shaft of grey rock runs down forever. Nobody has reached either end. People live on the walls, not the floor, because there is no floor. The whole population is a ring of cliff-dwellings lashed to the stone with rope bridges and old iron pins, and every house faces the middle.

Light comes from a slow lantern the size of a town, drifting down the shaft. It takes eleven days to pass, then eleven days of dark. During dark the crops are mushrooms and cave fish. During light the bridges hum with trade, and children race the lantern's edge to see who can touch the far side before it moves on.

The thing everyone knows and nobody fixes: the pins rust. The bridges hold anyway, mostly. When one drops, the neighborhood below just grows a new lower terrace and life continues one level down.

The only travelers are the Sinkers, who cut their ropes on purpose and fall to find out what is underneath. They send nothing back.

final: The world is called Lowtide, though it has no sea. Every forty days the ground remembers it was once water and forgets it was ground. For six hours the soil becomes a brine-saturated marsh, buildings sink to their second floor or float, and anything buried rises the way a body rises. The people who live here have built up, not out: towns are scaffolds, bridges, and ladders lashed to chimneys. Children learn rope before letters. The wealthy own stone platforms on stilts; the poor own nothing that can't be carried above their heads. The dead are a problem. A family's grandparents come back with the tide, walking, asking for tea, and the law says you must host them for one night or forfeit your roof. Most do. Some hire tide-merchants, who arrive with hooked poles and take the dead downriver to a pit no one maps. The pit has a name, but saying it is considered bad luck in the way that making a budget is bad luck. Magic is just the memory of water: runes that pool, spells that drip, wards that dry out and crack. A wizard's power is measured in cups, not spells. The moon is not visible. No one knows why. No one has asked in a long time.

A girl is the only person in her house who remembers anything — that the blue bowl is the cat's, that Tuesday is bin day, that Grandpa is called Frank and not "the tall one" — so she keeps the family's facts in a notebook with a string around it, because if she forgets the scarf is on the radiator hook nobody finds it and everyone stands in the hall shouting the same three words. The book is her notebook, page by page, and it is mostly not about her: it is about what a household actually runs on, which is one person noticing. The turn comes when she loses the notebook under the couch for a whole weekend and the family does not collapse into chaos but slowly, badly, manages — and she learns she is allowed to put it down sometimes, not because the notebook is unimportant but because it turns out other people can notice too, and did, quietly, the whole time. No villain, no magic, no tidy last line; just a kid, a string-bound book, and the ordinary weight of being the one who pays attention.

Quick question so I can aim it better: is this for a kid who is that child themselves, or for the grown-up who has one?

The Saltmarsh of Ommer Deep is a flat country where the tide comes in twice a day and leaves behind a crust of white salt that the villagers scrape up and sell by weight. Nobody owns the marsh. Each family owns the stakes, the wooden posts that mark where a plot ends, and the posts are repainted every spring with whatever color the family can afford. A red stake means a family in debt. A blue one means a widow runs the plot.

The main town, Quell, sits on stilts above the mud. Its market runs on a ledger kept by the salt-weighers, who write every sale in chalk on a slate hung from the bridge. The slate has been wiped and rewritten for four hundred years, and no one agrees on what the first entry said.

Beyond the marsh lies the Grey Cut, a channel that appeared after a storm and widens by a few paces each year. Boats that go into it do not always come out. The weighers say it is eating the salt, and they have started charging a toll to cross the bridge toward it.

The people of Ommer Deep speak in short sentences, count everything, and greet strangers by asking how much they weigh. It is considered rude to answer honestly.

The salt flats of Ossery stop at a wall of cranes that never finish building it. Every thirty years the wall moves a hand's width inland, and the people of the town of Dremmel keep a ledger of the gained ground in chalk on their doors.

Ossery is run by the Tallymen, who weigh the bones of drowned cattle to decide who may marry. Their scales hang in the square, and nobody says the word for "cheat" aloud, because the scales can hear it.

Outside the wall, the flats grow a pale grass that only blooms when someone lies to a child. Herders pay their debts in those flowers. A single bloom is worth a week of water.

The cranes are operated by a guild of deaf engineers who communicate by tapping on the iron. No one outside the guild has learned the tapping. Rumor says they are building something under the salt, and the ledger is not the wall's record but theirs.

Players arrive as salt-smugglers caught between the Tallymen's scales and the cranes' slow, patient gain.

The Saltmere Reaches are a drowned country. Three hundred years ago the sea came up through the old salt pans and swallowed the lowland villages, and what stayed above water became a chain of stilt towns linked by ferries that run on tallow and favors.

The people here do not say "flood." They say the water took the names. Every family keeps a ledger of the drowned: who was lost, what they owed, what they were promised. Debts pass down through the ledgers, so a child can inherit a grudge against a house that no longer stands.

Travel is by flat-bottomed boat, and every boat has a lantern with a painted eye at its prow. The eyes are for watching the reeds, where the eel-wives live. They trade in memories. A traveler who gives an eel-wife a true story leaves lighter, and one who lies leaves with a few of their own memories missing.

The old drowned cathedral still rings its bell at low tide. No one has climbed to it. The ferrymen say whoever reaches the bell will be paid in full, but the account is never said aloud.

Play here means paying what the water is owed, one ledger line at a time.

final: Harrow Vell is a lamplighter's widow who keeps the city's dead on the payroll: every drowned sailor, collapsed miner, and stillborn child is listed in a ledger, and each name, read aloud at the right hour, buys a family a single night of warmth in winter. She never asks for payment in coin. She asks for one small, true memory from each person who comes to her counter, a first bicycle-width thing like the smell of a particular bakery, and she writes it down under the dead man's name. Nobody notices the memories are gone until their own children ask them what the bakery smelled like. The villain's cruelty is patient and practical: she is not trying to rule anyone, only to keep the city's grief running like a debt that never gets paid off, and the people she helps are the ones who keep handing her more of themselves.

final: Maren Coole was the midwife of Ashwater for forty-one years, and she kept every ledger. Each birth, each mother, each price paid — recorded in her own hand, in a book nobody else was allowed to read. The town loved her; she had delivered most of them. What they never noticed was that the ledgers did not simply record. When a child died, Maren wrote the name anyway, and the name stayed alive in the book, and the parents went on having a child who came home at night and ate at their table and was not quite the one they had buried. She has three hundred and six of them now, all obedient, all grateful, all slowly forgetting how to be anything but hers. She is not cruel. She is tidy. And she has begun to think the town would be better if every child were entered in the book from the start, so nothing would ever be lost again.

final: Mireille Vantooth never learned to fight, because she learned something better: how to own people before they know they're for sale. She keeps a shop in the lower market that sells nothing you can see — just a ledger, a pen, and a chair that's always warm. **Job:** Night-shift dispatcher for a towing company that also runs the only 24-hour laundromat on Ferris Street. She works the phones from a folding chair behind the change machine.

**What she wants:** For the couple to finish a fight properly, out loud, before anyone leaves the building. She keeps a stopwatch on the counter and tells people when they've hit the minimum.

- Eats a single pickled egg before any emotional conversation, offers it to the male lead, and is offended when he declines.

She says, "You can't leave until the dryer finishes, that's Ferris Street law," and the whole room stops, because the dryer is on a six-minute cycle and she has just given the couple exactly six minutes to say the true thing.

**Why she steals the scene:** She is the only person who treats the romance as a practical problem with a deadline, and she is completely serious about it while everyone around her is falling apart.

- She has a rule that nobody leaves the laundromat until they have folded something together. She has broken it only twice, and both times it ended in a kiss.

**Her best line:** "I have seen you cry into a fitted sheet. The least you can do is let me watch you fall in love with it."

**Why she works:** She wants the romance as much as the audience does and will say so, bluntly, at the worst possible moment. She never steps out of the story to be funny. She just refuses to be ignored.

**Nell Kovacs, 44, funeral home receptionist.**

She's not the best friend, not the ex, not the wise neighbor. She's the woman who works the front desk at Ostrander & Sons, four blocks from where the leads keep having their terrible coffee dates, and she becomes the person both of them accidentally tell everything to because she is professionally unshockable. She has heard worse. She has heard worse *today*.

Nell's power is that she has no stake in the romance. She does not want them together, she does not want them apart, she wants the Henderson service to go smoothly at 2:00 and she wants the florist to stop substituting carnations. So when the female lead bursts in crying, Nell hands her a tissue from a box that exists for exactly this, listens, and says, "Okay. Do you want him to fix it, or do you want to be right?" — and the scene stops dead because nobody else in the movie is allowed to ask that.

How she steals scenes: she never raises her voice, she's always mid-task, and she says the true thing in the flattest tone. She also has one running bit — she keeps a list on a legal pad of "things people say at the worst moment of their life," not to mock them, just because she noticed the patterns. She never shows anyone the list. In the last act, someone finds it. Her entry about the male lead is one line and it's devastating.

Why she isn't a stock quirky sidekick: she doesn't perform for the audience, she doesn't dispense wisdom on cue, and she has a life the movie only glimpses — a teenage son who won't talk to her, a knee that needs surgery she keeps postponing. Her scenes land because she's the only character who treats the leads' crisis as a Tuesday.

Her best line, for a scene where the male lead is pacing the lobby at 11 p.m.: "You can sit. The dead don't mind, and I've got a while."

One question that would sharpen her: is she warm underneath, or is the flatness the real her? That changes whether she's a comfort or a mirror, and I'd write her differently depending on which one you want.

**NAME:** Birdy Nazzal
**AGE:** 60-ish, refuses to clarify
**OCCUPATION:** Overnight manager, "Lucky Seven" laundromat, 11 p.m. to 7 a.m.

Birdy does not enter scenes. She is already in them, and has been, and will be, long after your leads have finished their banter and gone home to think about each other.

This is why she steals every scene. The leads walk into the laundromat mid-argument about whether something counted as a date, and Birdy is there folding a stranger's towel with the slow, ceremonial patience of a woman who has all night and no intention of interrupting. She hears everything. She responds to nothing for ninety seconds. Then she says one sentence — flat, bored, devastating — and the argument is over because it has been rerouted through her.

**WHAT SHE WANTS:** Nothing from your leads. That's the engine. She has her own plot, running at all times, and it involves none of them. She is trying to get the folding table nearest the window re-tiled. She has been trying for four months. She mentions the tiling during a kiss. She mentions it during a confession. She mentions it when someone cries.

**THE MOVE:** Birdy gives terrible advice with total authority, and she knows it's terrible, and she's watching to see what they do with it anyway. She is running an experiment on the couple. She has run it before. She has notes.

**ONE HABIT:** Every night at 12:40 she buys one lottery ticket from the machine by the door. She never scratches it. She reads it. She keeps them in a shoebox, organized by date, and if you ask what they're for she says, "Documentation."

**WHY THE SCENE CANNOT LOSE HER:** She's the only person in any room who isn't performing for anyone. The leads are auditioning for each other. Birdy is just working. That stillness magnetizes the camera — and every director eventually notices the scene is now about whether Birdy will say something, not whether the couple gets together. Sometimes she never does.

The tiling never gets done. She is fine with this.

*One thing I'd need for a better fit: what kind of couple is at the center — are they young and loud, or older and quiet? Birdy's whole operational style (how hard she pushes, how much silence she uses) changes depending on who's across the folding table.*

Think about a group chat. You add three friends. Each of them adds three. Now there are twelve of you, and nobody did anything big — the invites just started inviting. That's why the chat hits 200 people by Friday when you only ever added three.

Compound interest works the same way with money. The interest you earn joins the pile and starts earning its own interest. Early on it's slow. Later, the pile is doing the inviting, and it gets loud fast.

The catch: this only happens if you leave it alone. Every time you pull money out, you're kicking people from the chat.

Your immune system runs on recognition. It can't fight what it can't name, and meeting a real virus is a costly way to learn a name — sometimes it learns too late.

A vaccine hands over the mugshot early. It's a dead virus, a fragment, a set of instructions for making one harmless piece. No illness, because nothing is trying to take over your cells.

Your body studies the face, builds cells that remember it, and files it away. If the real thing ever shows up, the response starts on day one instead of day five. Same defense, no head start for the intruder.

It isn't armor. It's a memory you didn't have to earn the hard way.

A locksmith gets a wax impression of a key without ever holding the key. He works from that alone — the ridges, the notch, the length — and cuts a blank to match. The real key never comes near him.

A vaccine is that wax impression. It's a harmless copy of some piece of the germ — a dead shell, a protein, a weakened version — enough for your body to read the shape. Your immune system studies the shape and cuts its own key: cells and antibodies shaped to fit that germ and nothing else.

Weeks later, if the real germ shows up, the key is already in the lock. Your body turns it before the germ gets far. Sometimes you feel tired or sore while the key is being cut. That's the work, not the disease.

Brand story:
The shop smells of wax and old paper. Most mornings Ilse unlocks the roller door at eight and finds a stack of chairs left on the step overnight, nobody's name on them.
